title: Correlation
intro: Interpret correlation, recognize its limits, and calculate it without confusing association with causation.

moments.title: What correlation measures
moments.text: Correlation summarizes direction and strength of a linear association.

moments.title: Zero correlation
moments.text: Zero correlation does not rule out a nonlinear association.

moments.title: Correlation and causality
moments.text: An association alone cannot establish a causal effect.

moments.title: Unusual points
moments.text: Adding or removing a point can change correlation.

moments.title: Calculate correlation
moments.text: Keep the two lists paired and inspect the scatterplot before interpreting r.

moments.title: Check the output
moments.text: Interpret a calculated correlation in the context of the data.

cards.name: Direction and strength
cards.text: The sign of $r$ gives direction; $|r|$ describes linear strength.

cards.name: Inspect first
cards.text: Curvature and unusual points can make a single correlation misleading, even if its magnitude is large.

cards.name: What it cannot establish
cards.text: Correlation does not establish causality or summarize arbitrary nonlinear relationships. Swapping x and y leaves r unchanged.

questions.obj: Interpret a correlation from paired data
questions.q: The video enters X values 5, 7, 12, 16, 20 and corresponding Y values 16.5, 18.9, 19.1, 21.6, 25.7. Calculate and interpret the correlation.

work.text: Each X value is matched to the Y value in the same position. Inspect their scatterplot for a roughly linear pattern.
Use the paired lists, not independently sorted columns.
The positive sign indicates Y tends to increase as X increases. The magnitude near 1 indicates a strong linear association for these data.

questions.answer: The five observations have a strong positive linear association. The coefficient alone does not show causality or guarantee model suitability.

questions.q: Supplementary example: one data set has correlation −0.88 and another has correlation 0.62. Compare their linear strength and direction.

work.text: The first association is negative and the second positive.
Linear strength depends on distance from zero.
The negative sign does not make an association weaker.

questions.answer: The −0.88 association is the stronger linear association; its response tends to decrease as the explanatory variable increases.

sections.title: Calculate and interpret correlation
sections.intro: Start with the empty calculator. Type each expression yourself; a video link reviews the underlying method.

steps.title: Enter paired lists
steps.suppose: we use the video's five paired observations.
steps.observe: Equal positions in the lists must refer to the same observation. Adjust the viewing window to see the points.

steps.title: Calculate the coefficient
steps.observe: The positive value describes a strong linear association for these five observations. The scatterplot still matters.

traps.title: A negative number is weaker
traps.better: The magnitude 0.9 indicates the stronger linear association; the sign gives direction.

traps.title: Zero means unrelated
traps.weak: A zero correlation proves there is no relationship.
traps.better: A strong curved relationship can have correlation near zero.

traps.title: Correlation proves a cause
traps.weak: A high correlation proves changing x causes y to change.
traps.better: Confounding and study design must be considered; correlation alone is not causal evidence.

questions.stem: Which coefficient describes the strongest linear association?
Converting both variables from meters to centimeters has what effect on correlation?
why: Positive changes of units do not scale r.
Positive unit conversions preserve direction and linear strength.

questions.stem: A curved U-shaped scatterplot has r near zero. Which is correct?
opts: There may still be a strong nonlinear association
The coefficient must be greater than 1
A straight-line model must be appropriate
why: r measures linear association, not all patterns.
Curvature can remain strong despite zero linear correlation.
Curvature argues against a straight-line model.

opts: A correlation with units of seconds
A correlation unchanged after swapping the variables
why: Correlation is symmetric in the two quantitative variables.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A study of storage batteries reports a correlation of −0.84 between age in months and run time in hours. Its scatterplot is approximately linear with no isolated points.
parts: (a) Interpret the direction and strength in context.
(b) Explain the effect on r of converting age to years and run time to minutes.
(c) Assess the claim that r proves battery age is the only cause of lower run time.
sample: (a) Older batteries tend to have shorter run times, with a strong negative linear association.
(b) Both changes are positive changes of units, so r remains −0.84.
(c) The correlation alone cannot establish causality, much less show age is the only cause. Other factors, such as usage history, may be related to both age and run time.
checklist: States a negative direction in context.
Describes linear strength using the magnitude.
Explains invariance under positive unit conversions.
Rejects the unsupported causal and sole-cause claims.
